# Chapter 16 - High-Performance Leadership and Management

## Research Findings

Through years of surveying technology professionals and writing State of DevOps Reports with Puppet, researchers identified what makes high-performing teams. Software delivery performance is critical because nearly every company relies on software. It is affected by leadership, tools, automation, and a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

## Book Structure

Part I presents research on why software delivery performance matters, driving organizational measures including profitability, productivity, market share, efficiency, effectiveness, customer satisfaction, and mission goals. The ability to deliver quality software at high tempo with stability is a key value driver regardless of size or industry. Part II summarizes the science behind the research, including design decisions and analysis methods. Part III addresses organizational change management, with contributions from colleagues Steve Bell and Karen Whitley Bell presenting what following these capabilities looks like for innovative organizations.

## Key Takeaways

Researchers identified key capabilities that contribute to software delivery performance in statistically significant ways. A critical caveat: you cannot buy or copy high performance—organizations must develop their own capabilities pursuing a path fitting their particular context and goals. This requires sustained effort, investment, focus, and time. However, the research is unequivocal: the results are worth it.

# Chapter 16 - High-Performance Leadership and Management

## Research Findings on High Performance

Over several years of surveying technology professionals and writing State of DevOps Reports with Puppet, the researchers discovered what makes high-performing teams and organizations. This journey included researching technology transformations, publishing peer-reviewed results, and collaborating with colleagues assessing and transforming their own organizations. A consistent finding: since nearly every company relies on software, delivery performance is critical to any organization. Software delivery performance is affected by many factors, including leadership, tools, automation, and a culture of continuous learning and improvement.

## Book Structure and Contributions

The book compiles findings across three parts. Part I presents research on why software delivery performance matters and how it drives organizational measures like profitability, productivity, market share, efficiency, effectiveness, customer satisfaction, and mission goals. The ability to deliver quality software at high tempo with stability is a key value driver and differentiator regardless of size or industry. Part II summarizes the science behind the research, including design decisions and analysis methods. Part III addresses organizational change management, with contributions from colleagues Steve Bell and Karen Whitley Bell presenting what following the outlined capabilities and practices looks like for innovative organizations.

## Key Takeaways

The researchers identified key capabilities contributing to software delivery performance in statistically significant and meaningful ways. Organizations are encouraged to use these findings to begin their own technology transformation. A critical caveat: you cannot buy or copy high performance—organizations must develop their own capabilities pursuing a path fitting their particular context and goals. This requires sustained effort, investment, focus, and time. However, the research is unequivocal: the results are worth it.

## Competitive Landscape Shift

Organizations across industries are moving away from large projects with long lead times toward small teams working in short cycles with user feedback. High performers continuously improve, accepting high risk and uncertainty.

## Four Imperatives for Acceleration

Organizations must accelerate: delivery of goods and services, market engagement to detect customer demand, anticipation of compliance changes, and response to risks (security threats, economic shifts). Software is central—banks trade faster, retailers offer superior selection and service, all enabled by technology. Bessen (2017) found strategic technology use explains revenue and productivity gains more than M&A or entrepreneurship.

## DevOps Transformation

DevOps emerged from organizations solving how to build secure, resilient, rapidly evolving distributed systems at scale. Examples include Netflix, Amazon, Google, Facebook, Capital One, Target, and US Digital Service. However, Forrester found 31% of the industry lacks practices like continuous integration/delivery, Lean, and collaborative culture (Stroud et al. 2017), while 47% of CEOs face board pressure to digitally transform (Panetta 2017). Organizations often overestimate their progress—executives especially so—suggesting greater value potential than realized and a need for accurate capability measurement.

## Capabilities vs. Maturity Models

Maturity models are inappropriate for four reasons: they imply a destination rather than continuous improvement; they prescribe linear "lock-step" solutions despite teams having different contexts; they measure technical proficiency without tying to outcomes (vanity metrics); and they define static levels without accounting for changing landscapes. Capability models are outcome-based, multidimensional, and dynamic—allowing organizations to focus on capabilities that drive improvement based on their specific context and goals.

## Evidence-Based Approach

Age, technology type, deployment ownership, and CAB implementation do NOT predict performance. The 24 key capabilities that drive improvement in software delivery and organizational performance are easy to define, measure, and improve.

## Performance Metrics

In 2017, high performers had 46 times more frequent deployments, 440 times faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170 times faster mean time to recover, and 5 times lower change failure rate than low performers. The tempo gap narrowed from 2016 while the stability gap widened—likely because low performers increased speed without building quality into the process. High performers achieve both speed and stability by building quality in.

# Chapter 1 - Accelerate

## The Need for Speed

Organizations must accelerate across four dimensions: delivery of goods and services, market engagement to detect customer demand, anticipation of compliance and regulatory changes, and response to risks including security threats and economic shifts. Software sits at the center of this acceleration across all industries—banks compete through faster, more secure trading and new customer channels; retailers win through superior selection, service, and seamless online/offline experiences.

The practices driving this transformation emerge from the DevOps movement, originally developed to solve wicked problems: building secure, resilient, rapidly evolving distributed systems at scale. Examples like Netflix, Amazon, Google, Facebook, Capital One, Target, and the US Federal Government's Technology Transformation Service and US Digital Service demonstrate that large enterprises with decades-old technologies also gain significant benefits.

## The Measurement Problem

Despite progress, 31% of the industry lacks foundational practices like continuous integration, continuous delivery, Lean practices, and collaborative culture (Stroud et al. 2017). Additionally, 47% of CEOs face board pressure to digitally transform (Panetta 2017). A key issue: executives overestimate their DevOps maturity compared to practitioners actually doing the work (Klavens et al. 2017). This gap suggests potential value is greater than executives realize and underscores the need for accurate capability measurement.

## Capabilities Over Maturity

The authors argue strongly against maturity models for four reasons: they imply a destination rather than continuous improvement; they prescribe lock-step, linear progression rather than customized approaches; they often measure vanity metrics unrelated to outcomes; and they ignore the ever-changing technology landscape. Capability models are multidimensional, outcome-based, and dynamically adaptable.

## What Actually Drives Performance

Surprisingly, neither application age, technology type (mainframe vs. greenfield), who performs deployments, nor change approval board (CAB) implementation predicted performance. Instead, 24 key capabilities drive improvement in both software delivery and organizational performance.

## The Performance Gap

2017 research revealed high performers have 46 times more frequent deployments, 440 times faster lead time from commit to deploy, 170 times faster mean time to recover, and 5 times lower change failure rate than low performers. Notably, the gap narrowed for tempo but widened for stability from 2016 to 2017, suggesting low performers increased speed without building in quality. High performers avoid trading speed for stability by building quality into their processes.

# Chapter 2 - Measuring Performance

## Flaws in Prior Measurement Approaches

**Lines of Code (LOC)**: Rewarding LOC leads to bloated software with higher maintenance costs. The Apple Lisa team discovered LOC was meaningless when developers logged "negative 2000 lines of code."

**Velocity**: Used in Agile to measure story points completed per iteration. Flaws include: (1) it's relative and team-dependent, making cross-team comparison invalid; (2) teams game estimates by inflating them and prioritizing their own throughput over cross-team collaboration.

**Utilization**: High utilization eliminates slack to absorb unplanned work. Queue theory shows that as utilization approaches 100%, lead times approach infinity—making teams exponentially slower.

## Four Key Metrics

Valid measures must focus on global outcomes and measure outcomes rather than outputs.

**Delivery Lead Time**: Time from code committed to successfully running in production. Options ranged from "less than one hour" to "more than six months."

**Deployment Frequency**: Batch size is hard to measure in software, so deployment frequency serves as a proxy. Options ranged from "on demand (multiple deploys per day)" to "fewer than once every six months."

**Time to Restore Service**: In rapidly changing systems, failure is inevitable; the key question is restoration speed.

**Change Fail Rate**: Percentage of production changes resulting in degraded service or requiring remediation (hotfix, rollback, fix-forward, or patch).

## Cluster Analysis Findings

Using cluster analysis across all four years (2014–2017), three distinct groups emerged: high, medium, and low performers. All four measures served as good classifiers.

**Key finding**: High performers do better at *all* measures—there is no tradeoff between improving performance and achieving stability/quality. This aligns with Lean and Agile predictions but contradicts industry assumptions about trading speed for reliability.

**Year-over-year trends**: High performers maintained or improved from 2016 to 2017. Low performers increased throughput only in 2017 after stagnant levels from 2014–2016, while losing stability—likely from attempting to work faster without addressing underlying obstacles.

**2016 anomaly**: Medium performers had worse change fail rates than low performers, possibly due to mid-transformation rearchitecture challenges and accumulating technical debt from prioritizing new work over critical rework.

## Impact on Organizational Performance

High-performing organizations were **twice as likely** to exceed goals in profitability, market share, and productivity (validated scale from Widener 2007, correlated with ROI). In 2017, high performers were also twice as likely to exceed objectives in goods/service quantity, operating efficiency, customer satisfaction, quality, and mission goals (validated scale from Cavalluzzo and Ittner 2004).

Small-batch delivery enables rapid user feedback via A/B testing and experimental approaches—highly correlated with continuous delivery practices. This provides a strong argument against outsourcing strategic software development.

## Driving Change

These metrics enable evidence-based decisions, benchmarking, and hypothesis testing. For example, change management boards do *not* improve performance—they are negatively correlated with tempo and stability.

However, measurement tools require careful use. As Deming stated: "whenever there is fear, you get the wrong numbers." In pathological or bureaucratic cultures, measurement becomes control; people hide information. Learning culture must precede scientific improvement approaches.

# Chapter 2 - Measuring Performance

## Defining Valid Software Delivery Metrics

Measuring software performance is difficult because inventory is invisible, work breakdown is arbitrary, and design and delivery happen simultaneously. The authors sought to define "good" software delivery performance scientifically.

## Flaws in Prior Measurement Approaches

**Lines of Code (LOC)**: Rewarding LOC leads to bloated software with higher maintenance costs. The ideal is solving problems with minimum code—or no code at all. The Apple Lisa team story illustrates this: management discovered LOC was meaningless when developers logged "negative 2000 lines of code."

**Velocity**: Used in Agile to measure story points completed per iteration. Flaws include: (1) it's relative and team-dependent, making cross-team comparison invalid; (2) teams game estimates by inflating them and prioritizing their own throughput over cross-team collaboration.

**Utilization**: High utilization eliminates slack to absorb unplanned work or changes. Queue theory shows that as utilization approaches 100%, lead times approach infinity—making teams exponentially slower.

## Four Key Metrics

A valid performance measure must focus on global outcomes (not local optimization) and measure outcomes rather than outputs.

**Delivery Lead Time**: Reinertsen calls the design phase the "fuzzy front end" due to unclear start points and high variability. The authors measured delivery lead time: time from code committed to successfully running in production. Survey options ranged from "less than one hour" to "more than six months."

**Deployment Frequency**: Batch size is hard to measure in software, so deployment frequency serves as a proxy. Options ranged from "on demand (multiple deploys per day)" to "fewer than once every six months." Deployment frequency is the reciprocal of batch size.

**Time to Restore Service**: In rapidly changing systems, failure is inevitable; the key question is restoration speed. Same response options as lead time.

**Change Fail Rate**: Percentage of production changes resulting in degraded service or requiring remediation (hotfix, rollback, fix-forward, or patch).

## Cluster Analysis Findings

Using cluster analysis across all four years of research (2014–2017), the authors identified three distinct performance groups: high, medium, and low performers. All four measures served as good classifiers, and groups differed significantly across all measures.

**Key finding**: There is no tradeoff between improving performance and achieving stability/quality. High performers do better on *all* measures. This aligns with Agile and Lean predictions but contradicts industry assumptions about trading speed for reliability.

**Year-over-year trends**: High performers maintained or improved from 2016 to 2017. Low performers increased throughput only in 2017 after maintaining the same level from 2014–2016, while losing ground in stability—likely from attempting to work faster without addressing underlying obstacles.

**2016 anomaly**: Medium performers had worse change fail rates than low performers. Possible explanation: medium performers were mid-transformation, dealing with rearchitecture challenges, accumulating technical debt by prioritizing new work over critical rework.

## Impact on Organizational Performance

High-performing organizations were **twice as likely** to exceed goals in profitability, market share, and productivity (validated scale from Widener 2007, correlated with ROI). In 2017, high performers were also twice as likely to exceed objectives in goods/service quantity, operating efficiency, customer satisfaction, quality, and mission goals (validated scale from Cavalluzzo and Ittner 2004).

Small-batch delivery enables rapid user feedback via A/B testing and experimental approaches—highly correlated with continuous delivery technical practices. This provides a strong argument against outsourcing strategic software development.

## Driving Change

These metrics enable evidence-based decisions, benchmarking, and hypothesis testing. The authors can test which practices actually impact delivery performance—including testing assumptions like whether change management boards improve performance (they do not; negatively correlated with tempo and stability).

However, measurement tools require careful use. As Deming stated: "whenever there is fear, you get the wrong numbers." In pathological or bureaucratic cultures, measurement becomes control; people hide information. Learning culture must precede scientific improvement approaches.

# Appendix C: Statistical Methods Used in Our Research

## Overview

This appendix describes the statistical methods and procedures used to analyze survey data and test hypotheses about software delivery performance and organizational outcomes. The research team employed structural equation modeling (SEM) and partial least squares (PLS) path modeling as primary analytical techniques.

## Survey Development and Validation

Survey items underwent psychometric validation, including assessment of reliability (using Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability) and validity (including convergent and discriminant validity). The research team used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to validate measurement models and assessed common method variance using Lindell and Whitney's (2001) marker variable technique.

## Analytical Approach

The analysis employed PLS-SEM, chosen because the research involved both reflective and formative constructs, and the dataset did not meet assumptions for covariance-based SEM. The team report results using effect sizes (f²), predictive relevance (Q²), and model fit indices following guidelines from Hair et al. (2006), Chin (2010), and Gefen and Straub (2005). They report path coefficients, t-statistics from bootstrapping (5000 resamples), and R² values for endogenous constructs.

## Hierarchical Regression and Moderation

The research used hierarchical regression to test control variables and examine interaction effects, following procedures described in Cohen et al. (1983). Moderation effects were tested using interaction terms and separate group analyses as recommended by Chin, Marcolin, and Newsted (2003), who provide detailed guidance for interaction effects in PLS based on their Monte Carlo simulation study.

## Model Specification Testing

Model comparison used Ward's (1963) method of hierarchical clustering to identify distinct organizational profiles. The team compared alternative models using SRMR (Standardized Root Mean Square Residual) and other fit indices to assess specification quality.
